extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and methods for dramatizing a character's consciousness in novels, including when to use first-person, epistolary forms, or authorial withdrawal to 'show' rather than 'tell'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of first-person autobiography when the story centers on the narrator's inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man in the book is expected to make a searching and elaborate portrait of himself, the dramatizing force of the first person 'gives out' — the hero's mere report is inadequate to render 'what it was like to be' him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on an autobiographical narrator to render the protagonist's inner life when the subject's centre of gravity is that inner life; consider substituting a method that dramatizes the consciousness directly so the reader can judge for themselves. Example: Meredith's Harry Richmond shows the limit of autobiography; Strether (Henry James) demonstrates a stronger dramatized mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person when the narrator functions as a pictorial seeing-eye
rubrics_metrics.description: First person is useful 'for enhancing the value of a picture' where a selecting, interpreting, composing minister (a narrator) is required to present the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ first-person narration when the story needs an identifiable storyteller who interprets the scene for us and whose presence enhances pictorial richness — but only when the story's subject is external to the narrator rather than the narrator's own inner drama. Example: Thackeray's Vanity Fair benefits from knowing who the story-teller is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a character's consciousness (make the mind visible and active)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of receiving a report, 'we now see him in the act of judging and reflecting; his consciousness... is before us in its original agitation.' The character's interior life should be cast into the world of independent, rounded objects and made to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent impulses, judgments, and mental movements as scenes or surface actions so the reader experiences the mind 'in the theatre' rather than as a summarized account. Example models: Strether in The Ambassadors; Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the more dramatic (indirect/showing) method where the subject allows it
rubrics_metrics.description: The indirect, dramatic way 'places the thing itself in view, instead of recalling and reflecting and picturing it.' For any story there is an ideal point on the line of progress towards drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push the method toward drama (showing rather than telling) until no further dramatic gain accrues; choose the most emphatic dramatizing method the subject permits to let people and action 'appear independently'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: do not over-treat or under-treat the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method 'is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further.' A story is damaged by too much treatment as by too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance dramatic method and authorial restraint according to the subject: if increased dramatization would displace the subject (e.g., David Copperfield), refrain. Let the subject determine how far to dramatize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the subject to determine point of view and manner of telling
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is indicated by the subject of the story itself; the author is guided by a twofold consideration — making the story speak for itself and economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the subject 'needs the seeing eye' of a particular character or can be rendered scenically; select point of view that best brings out the subject while conserving economy and dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the epistolary/diary method to capture contemporaneous emotion, but beware its drawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: A running diary or series of letters can 'show a mind in action' and keep an ordeal 'always in the foreground', giving immediacy and recurring suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider epistolary forms to dramatize ongoing emotion (Clarissa, Grandison), but be cautious of verisimilitude strains and contrivances required to keep characters isolated or forced to communicate only by letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render inner thought by its surface movements rather than by authoritative exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist can 'represent it by means of the movement that flickers over the surface of his mind' — impulses, reactions, and momentary images become the players on the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the 'look and behaviour of thought' visible: show passing images, ripples, impulses, and small scenes of reflection so the mind tells its story through surface manifestation rather than direct exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial withdrawal: refrain from supplying extraneous authorial knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Henry James 'most carefully refrains from using his knowledge' of Strether; the author should accept nothing for the reader on authority and leave the mind's surface to teach the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdraw the author's interpretive voice when dramatization suffices; avoid stepping in to explain or to disclose secrets that would otherwise be inferred by watching the character's mind unfold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve suspense by gradual revelation rather than full disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author or narrator begins to expound the substance of a mind 'he must at once give us the whole of it' — which undermines suspense. Dramatization allows 'the story in it [the mind] to be played out by due degrees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing consciousness, withhold full inner explanation and reveal the character's changes in stages (glimpses, ripples) so the reader experiences suspense and discovery as in drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making a narrator the man who cannot be a narrator without betraying essential secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: In a tale of murder, 'there is one man who cannot possibly be the narrator, and that is the murderer himself' — because if he narrates he must reveal what the reader should be guessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose narrators whose necessary knowledge would destroy the story's dramatic tension or surprise; select a point of view that preserves necessary ignorance where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled shifting of point of view to situate the reader advantageously
rubrics_metrics.description: In The Ambassadors 'there is an insidious shifting of [point of view], so artfully contrived that the reader may arrive at the end without suspecting the trick' — placing the reader in a better position for understanding than the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ subtle, controlled shifts in perspective to give readers access to the material needed for understanding while maintaining dramatization and authorial discretion; ensure shifts are motivated and do not break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator stand between reader and living drama unless for a necessary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible' — do not let the hero or heroine 'stand in front of her emotions and portray them — unless for cause, for some needful effect that would otherwise be missed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only retain an intervening narrator or retrospective reflection when it serves a particular, necessary artistic or thematic purpose (e.g., Barry Lyndon). Otherwise prioritize immediate dramatic presentation of emotions and thought.
